essay_title: Alltäglichkeit, Timefulness, in the Heideggerian Program
author: Nancy S. Struever
essay_thesis: Aristotle's *Rhetoric* — read in Heidegger's SS 1924 lectures as the 'first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of being-with-one-another' — supplies Heidegger with a *life science* whose distinctive contribution is a politicized, biologized account of *time* as the irreducible 'timefulness' (Alltäglichkeit) of Dasein, against any timeless philosophical *epistēmē* — and rhetoric thereby colonizes the philosophical program of *Being and Time* from within.

epigraphs.text: Rhetorik ist nichts anderes als die Auslegung des konkreten Daseins, die Hermeneutik des Dasein selbst.
Rhetorik [ist] ... die erste systematische Hermeneutik der Alltäglichkeit des Miteinanderseins

hierarchical_outline.heading: I. THE PLACE OF RHETORIC IN THE ARISTOTELIAN PROGRAM: LIFE AND TIMES
argumentative_moves: Frames SS 1924 as 'extraordinary opportunity for the historian of rhetoric' (p. 105) — the lectures use *Rhetoric* to gloss the *Grundbegriffe* (basic concepts) of being, good, virtue, happiness, end, potency/act

Establishes that rhetoric for Heidegger is *not* a *technē* of manipulating discourse but operates *innerhalb der politikē* (inside politics, GA 18 134) — rhetoric is internal to political life, not adjacent to it

Catalogues Heidegger's strategies: rhetoric as life-science, intricated with biology (*Parts of Animals*, *Motion of Animals*, GA 18 207–219); rhetoric as motion/change study (*Physics* III, 200b12 = GA 18 284 *archē kinēseōs kai metabolēs*); kairos/kinesis/dynamis/entelechia/energeia (GA 18 195) all operative
Identifies *Alltäglichkeit* as the 'vital time dimension of Dasein' (the concept's working definition for the essay)

subsections.heading: 1. Heidegger's Account of the Nature of Rhetorical Inquiry: Rhetoric as Life Science
argumentative_moves: Anchored by SS 1924 epigraph: 'Daß wir die aristotelische "Rhetorik" haben, ist besser, als wenn wir eine Sprachphilosophie hätten' — having Aristotle's *Rhetoric* is better than having a philosophy of language

Adopts Aubenque's reading of *Rhetoric* as 'fully rhetorized psychology' with topics already organized for argument; Heidegger intricates *pathē*, *orexis*, *prohairesis*, *hexis*, *Besorgen* with rhetoric's strategic concerns (*pistis*, *doxa*, *endoxa*, *topoi*, *enthymēma*)

Crucial Heidegger move: lectures on *doxa* (GA 18 136–158) show rhetor's purpose is to push Dasein into *doxa* — continuous pragmatic engagement with time, *Alltäglichkeit* (GA 18 136). Cites *De anima* 428a 20–21 for the *doxa*/*pistis* relation; *doxa* as *Ja-sagen* (affirmation, 137); 'Die *doxa* ist die Weise, in der wir das Leben in seiner Alltäglichkeit da haben' (138)
Defines *doxa* as *Orientierung* (orientation/refocusing); rhetoric's strength lies in concern with *Aussagen* (articulation) — speaking-for the community (109–136)
Aligns with Klaus Dockhorn: rhetoric is not a teaching-manuals tradition but a 'second formation, indeed alternate formation to philosophy in the classical period'

Closing thesis-of-section: 'For Heidegger rhetoric is not a *technē*, the inauthentic definition (114), but a potentiality for theorizing, a *dynamis tou theoresai* (1355b26, GA 18 122)' — *not an energeia, an actuality* but a potential, *peculiar time-fraughtness*; rhetoric describes 'the radical incompleteness, the unending, time-ridden task of politics'; *legein* as *pithanon* (116) marks rhetoric as 'irrevocably timebound'

subsections.heading: 2. Rhetoric and Politics: Time and Motion Studies
argumentative_moves: Opening syllogism (Heidegger's): 'If life, then motion, *kinēsis* (286). If motion, then time. If the basic concern of life studies is movement, *Sein-als-Bewegtsein* (286), then the primary strategies of rhetoric must deal with time'
Reads SS 1924 lectures on *pathos* as long meditation on Aristotle, *Rhet*. 1378a19–21 ('emotions are all those feelings that so change men as to affect their judgements [*kriseis*]')

*Kinesis* gives 'authentic Da-Charakter to Dasein, the vital place-time of Being' (GA 18 287); ontological significance of passions = our capacity for change, *Veränderlichkeit* of Being; passions as *veränderliche Beschaffenheit* (167)

Passions are not *Wissen* but *Befindlichkeiten* (232) — dispositions; they are dispositions oriented on others' dispositions: 'Das *eidos* der *pathē* ist ein Sichverhalten zu anderen Menschen, ein In-der-Welt-Sein' (GA 18 207). The rhetor is 'oriented to the hearer's dispositions (121, 250)... to bring Dasein into *doxa*, make us "take to heart" an opinion. Thus *logos* functions only in a Dasein defined as a lively practice of doxa, and of cares, and of passions'

Long passage on *phobos* (GA 18 246–261): fear's 'peculiar tense, voice, and mode' = future, voice subjunctive, mode the possible. *Phobos* as 'already there' (276) as *Boden*, 'ground' (276). *Phobos bouleutikous poiei* (1382b21–22, GA 18 259–260): fear makes us deliberators. Fear as *pistis* (belief), *pathos* (disposition) is essential to rhetorical analysis

subsections.heading: 3. Time is of the Essence: Heidegger's Formulation of Alltäglichkeit
argumentative_moves: Heidegger contrasts the philosophic obsession with timeless truths (*aei on*, 140) and rhetoric's *Zeitlichkeit* — 'rhetoric handles, discloses the "Miteinandersprechen im Sinne des alltäglichen Miteinanderredens" (155)'

Rhetoric's interest in *Aussagen*, articulation, develops 'an account of life in its dailiness, its timefulness, its radical specificity of time, its care for tense': 'Das Sein in sich selbst als Besorgen und besorgendes Sprechen ist *zeitlich*, besorgt das *noch-nicht-Vorhandene*, spricht über das *schon-Geschehene*, betrachtet das *Jetzt-Daseiende*' (GA 18 131)
Three rhetorical genres are explications of three temporal orientations: deliberative (future policies); judicial (past justice/injustice); epideictic (shared values of the present)

*Kairos*: the Hellenic primary canon; measure of time, the moment, the response to it; *to prepon* (Greek), *quod decet* (Latin) — for dealing with the radical contingency of practical life. Kairos is 'the indispensable... term of Heidegger's account of the Aristotelian *Grundbegriffe*' (140)

Long discussion of *meson*/*hexis*/*kairos*: ethics needs *chronos* but 'Die Zeitcharakter der *ēthikē* liegt in *pollakis*' (GA 18 194) — frequency, not duration. *Meson für die praxis ist der kairos* (144) = 'sharp commentary on the virtue of prudence'. Heidegger shifts *meson* from medicine (geometric/arithmetic) to ethics: *meson* is *Jeweiligkeit* (temporal particularity, 'particular while' / 'respective Dasein', 201)

*Hexis*: the *Grundbestimmung* of *aretē* (185) — basic to Aristotelian ethics. Hexis is dynamis, *Gefasstsein* (185) — a potential for having; not pure duration but timebound, acquired and lost; *energeia, das eigentliche Da, das Gegenwärtigsein des Habenden und des Gehabten*; the having of *hekaston*, specific *pathē* as dispositions (192); *hexis* is *ein Wie des pathos* (GA 18 184); movement from potency to act describes basic dimension of moral agency

Closing: timefulness pervades rhetorical argument structure. *Topoi* and *endoxa* are revisable (138) — *Revisionsfähigkeit* — 'as opposed to the *epistēmē* which is not revisable'; Aristotle's grasp of foreshortened rhetorical argument because audience 'takes more to heart' short chains (133); *apeiron* (the boundless, 292) undermines philosophical arguments devoted to maintaining stability — 'foundationalist accounts of Greek ethics are late, extraneous applications of the Grundbegriffe... life phenomena described in rhetoric's timeliness do not stand under theoretical axioms (132)'

subsections.heading: 4. Alltäglichkeit as Qualification of Miteinandersein
argumentative_moves: Heidegger's antifoundationalism = continuous motion implies continuous impurity. Aristotle attributes passions to the *whole person*, not just the soul (GA 18 122, 192, 197); the formula *Seele als ousia* specifies *Sein eines Lebenden* (30), 'both notes and relegates Aristotle's entification' — a rejection of mind-as-cabinet-of-consciousness

'Mind is not at all pure': '*Das noein des Menschen ist kein reines* (202). It is dependent upon imagination, among other faculties, and imagination is, of course, dependent upon bodily sensation; imagination is the *Boden* of *noein* (199). Thus impurity supports *Alltäglichkeit*, timefulness, as hermeneutical focus; impurity prejudices pure duration'

Volume-defining sentence: 'In the SS 1924 program, temporality corrodes foundationalism, and *Alltäglichkeit* is the catalytic agent of temporality. In the definition of rhetoric in *Being and Time*, *Alltäglichkeit* is the primary qualification of *Miteinandersein*. Rhetorical interests thus must support equal and heavy emphasis on temporality and interaction'

Coining the title's term: 'Alltäglichkeit defines everydayness not as "ordinary" but as "timefulness," the timely character of practical life: it designates the continuous, if intermittent, repetitious demands of daily life, its iterability. "Miteinandersein" stipulates as primitive, ineluctable, living-with-one-another. Man is not self-sufficient (96); life, any life, is there (da) for another being (241)'

Comparison with Hobbes (GA 18 207): 'Heidegger defines the passions as intrinsically social, interpersonal, rather than simply physiological' — *ein Sichverhalten zu anderen Menschen*. Cites Dumouchel: emotions are 'qualifications of life-in-the-world' (GA 18 46–47); per Hobbes/Heidegger, an emotion 'attribut[ed] to a person is a performative, a political deed'

Closes section I with 'politics of hearing': 'Das Sprechen sein telos hat beim "Hörer," beim akroatēs' (GA 18 123); 'Das akouein, "Hören," ist die eigentliche aisthesis' (104). The hearer defines speaker's task. Heidegger's account of hearing (169) explores temporality as qualifying response; rhetoric's commitment to hearing > speaking. Aristotle: primacy of hearer in determining rhetorical *telos* (1358b1). Cites Cassin/Narcy on *Met*. 1006a24–26 — responsibility for argument's success rests with listener (*hypomenon*), not the demonstrator (*apodeiknys*)

hierarchical_outline.heading: II. MEDITATIONS ON TIME
argumentative_moves: Pivots from rhetoric-as-Aristotelian-life-science (Section I) to a meta-question: what kind of time-revisionism does Heidegger's rhetorical reading produce? Where does it sit in the 20th-century revisions of time (Husserl, Dilthey, Blattner)?
Argues SS 1924's rhetorical *Alltäglichkeit* anticipates and seeds the temporal innovations of *Being and Time* (1927); rhetoric 'colonizes' BT's philosophical program from within

subsections.heading: 1. Making a Place for Rhetoric in the History of Inquiry
argumentative_moves: Anchored by SS 1924 epigraph: 'Es gilt nicht Neues zu sagen, sondern das zu sagen, was die Alten schon meinten' — what is at issue is not saying something new but saying what the ancients already meant

Rhetoric for Heidegger has 'three important, and somewhat counterintuitive qualities: rhetoric is "better than a *Sprachphilosophie*" (117); it is not simply a purely formal verbal *technē*; and it exists inside politics' — combination ensures rhetoric is 'a most basic hermeneutic of "Dasein selbst"' since vital life capacity is discursive

Aristotle 'corrects Plato'; *Rhetoric* has 'great revisionary force'. Plato 'misses' Dasein (37) but Aristotle 'gets Socrates right' (184), 'gives a better account of Greek doxa' (140). Hellenistic/medieval rhetoric became a *school* discipline (110)

Aristotle's careful analysis of *pathē* in *Rhet.* 2 connects to heavy influence of rhetorical *Affektenlehre* on Stoa (122) and Christian theology from patristic period through Thomas and Luther (177)
Cites Wilhelm Dilthey as the only modern thinker who recognized this 'vital historical initiative' (177–178)

subsections.heading: 2. Time in and as Discipline
argumentative_moves: *Rhetoric* corrects Heideggerian inquiry by raising the issue of timely development. While Heidegger may have thought he 'effaced rhetoric in his new philosophical program of *Being and Time*, rhetoric effectively colonized his philosophy from within' (volume-key claim)

Rhetorical accounts are 'qualities of incarnate, interactive timefulness' (n. 23); 'Rhetorical inquiry is corrective because of its temporal values, that is, time is corrective. Again, dailiness destroys theoretical complacency (130–131), and theory grows out of *Alltäglichkeit* (66)'

Heidegger cites *epistēmē* and dialectic; rhetoric is *paraphyes* (offshoot) of dialectic and ethics; *antistrophē* of dialectic (125–130); intervention of rhetorical time occurs between Aristotelian *epistēmē* (timeless, *aei on* 140) and Heidegger's qualification 'Ich verstehe gar nicht den Seinscharakter der *epistēmē*, wenn ich nicht das Wovon [*pros ti*] in Betracht ziehe' (324) — what 'science' is must depend on what it is 'science of'

'Rather than absorption in a timeless truth, rhetorical discipline depends on dailiness; rhetorical practice makes public, *offenbar*, or *sichtbar* (136), the true, *Wahr*, in the verisimilar, *wahrscheinlich* (122)'

*Logos* as *horismos* is not *alltäglich* (36); the daily speech, *legein*, has enunciation as object, *Grundbestimmung* (114), but does not *define* (*horizein*); 'Heidegger thus problematizes the task of definition of concepts, the ostensible subject of SS 1924'

Important analogy: like medicine, rhetoric does not address particular individuals (Socrates/Callias) but invents problematic — and unlike medicine has no domain of expertise, is not a *technē* (114). Cites *De anima* 433a3–6 — distance between knowledge of healing and healing itself; 'life as *praxis* has nothing to do with *technē* (183); rhetorical pragmatism is investigation, not instrument'
Closing: 'when we lost Greek rhetoric, we lost Greek politics'

subsections.heading: 3. Modern Times: Specific Twentieth-Century Revisions of Time
subsections.epigraph: There is no mechanical truth in saying the past determines the future, rather than the future the past. — C.S. Peirce, 'Reply to the Necessitarians'
argumentative_moves: Pivots to Blattner/Dilthey/Husserl: how do Heidegger's Aristotelian rhetorical initiatives prepare his BT temporal work?

subsections.heading: A. Manifolds
argumentative_moves: Anchored on Blattner: Dasein's temporality is 'non-sequential manifold of future, present, and past', complex simultaneity. BT Division I innovations represent 'fundamental commitment in Heidegger's theory to a temporal manifold, rather than to a linear sequence of past, present, and future "nows"'
Heidegger in SS 1924 'found a very different account of temporality within the political parameters of the *Rhetoric*' enabling sense of time as simultaneous, intricated, experientially complex

Per Blattner: 'our time, Heidegger discovers, if accounted for minutely, is not at all ordinary, not at all the contentless, vapid flow of a succession of nows stipulated for our philosophy by the contemporary mathematical models'
Coining: 'In SS 1924 Aristotle "improves on" Plato in his rhetorical account of the experience of time; the definitions produced are a Greek ontology *in nuce*, of being in motion (321)'

BT definitions of tense: 'future is not "out there," off someplace, nor is the past'; future is not a now in succession but 'coming to be' as process. Aristotle's *dynamis* reformulated in BT as 'pressing ahead into,' 'for the sake of which' (n. 29 = Blattner 109)

*Purposiveness, readiness, ambition* are key concepts (n. 30): potentialities, capacities rather than complete, finished actualities (contrast Aristotelian *energeia*). For past affectivity is central: 'the facticity of the past is a lingering, affect is *schon da* (n. 31 = Blattner 112)' — recall Heidegger's intricate presentation of tense in Aristotle's account of fear in SS 1924
Habit (with connotations of duration and past presence) described in SS 1924 as process, 'present-ing,' a *Gegenwärtigen des Habenden* (175); Greek focus on present as 'making present' (192)

Blattner contrast: BT's 'apolitical?' erosion of *Alltäglichkeit* into ordinariness; vs. SS 1924 where rhetoric is the explanatory mode for hearing — rhetorical *Alltäglichkeit* still has political/temporal richness; 'politics requires simultaneous consideration of past, present, and future dimensions of political action and choice. In politics there is no pure present, no unmotivated future, no isolated past. It is a political manifold'

subsections.heading: B. Realism in Aristotle, Dilthey, and Husserl?
argumentative_moves: Per Makkreel: Dilthey's temporality is realist; Dilthey's time derived from *Innewerden* (inner becoming), not Kantian *Vorstellen* (representative consciousness). 'Dilthey rejects... the claim that time is the ideal form of inner experience.'

Heidegger uses Aristotle's *Rhetoric* to gloss the centrality of life experience in his own theory, and 'in Aristotle — demonstrated in his intrication of the biological texts such as *Parts of Animals* with the *Rhetoric* in the lectures'
Heidegger's insistence Aristotle's life is nothing 'wild or deep or mystical' echoes Dilthey's foundational concepts being those of 'life itself' (n. 37 = Rodi 114–115)

Dilthey, Husserl, and Heidegger 'focus on time for us, on a manifold of lived, not conceptualized time'; the *Rhetoric* in SS 1924 'gives a classical justification for the investigative habits of the psychological and phenomenological research of the early twentieth century'

subsections.heading: C. SS 1924 and SS 1925: 'The History of the Concept of Time'
argumentative_moves: Per Kisiel's account of SS 1925 GA 20 *Prolegomena zur Geschichte des Zeitbegriffs*: time is the temporality of Dasein; rhetoric's *Alltäglichkeit* offers 'a way into the problematic'

Per Dilthey: time is 'whirring away' inside consciousness, not outside framework — but consciousness ready to be defined as Dasein, 'a manifold of co-original structures, ways of being'; care as primary structure (totality) of constitution of Dasein's being

SS 1925 contains 'brief, but significant, intrusion of rhetoric, where Heidegger defines rhetoric as "the first part of logic, rightly understood"' (n. 41 = GA 20 264) and 'diffuse echoes of the rhetorical formulae of SS 1924: there is the connection of language, life, and truth, since life is language capacity (the Aristotelian *zoon logon echon*); thus life capacity is political capacity, and thus discourse as social practice, *Miteinanderreden*, has priority over language as concept'
Closing: 'in SS 1925 a recollection of a rhetorical politics of language, an investigational initiative that underwrites the politics of time'

subsections.heading: 4. Special Effects of the Rhetorical Connection: Politics First
argumentative_moves: Heidegger's *use* of *Rhetoric* is consequential — not simply prominence in lectures on *Grundbegriffe*. The 'quintessentially rhetorical initiative in the development of temporality is the focus on the politics of time'

Two Aristotelian statements that Heidegger contrasts: (1) 'Die Ethik gehört in die Politik' (GA 18 127) = ethics belongs to politics; (2) 'Rhetorik... steht innerhalb der politikē' (134) = rhetoric is inside politics. (1) conveys ethical issues are originary and enduring problematic; (2) conveys rhetoric is investigation of possible political uses of technique — intrinsic, not dependent

*Rhetoric* 2: creation/alteration/reception of *doxa, endoxa, pathē, prohairesis, pisteis, krisis* exhausts limited repertoire of political acts; 'rhetorical material does not stand under, or derive from theoretical axioms; insofar as rhetoric locates elemental functions specifically, it epitomizes political action, rather than supplements a general preexistent theory. Or rhetoric, in terms of Hellenic task, is prephilosophical in a strong sense'

Two effects of integrated political/rhetorical interests: (1) *meson* defined as *Jeweiligkeit* is functional, not immoral — Dasein experiences only appropriate or inappropriate nows, the right time or wrong time; coordinated social practices (n. 43 = Blattner 67, 73, 131–133); (2) constancy of change — passion's basic nature as disposition is changeability (Meyer)

'Rhetoric gives us the means for and the analysis of authenticity. And there is no part of the political that does not manifest the constraints of time. In sum, a Heideggerian politics of time appears, even if briefly, in SS 1924 — a politics perhaps hypothesized by Arendt in her early fascination with Heidegger'

Engagement with Stanley Fish on 'inspired adhoccery' — multiculturality crisis demands case-by-case improvisation; Fish's failure: insufficient temporality. Cicero (*De legibus*) on Roman law's 'continuous identity' achieved by 'great ingenuity' in particular cases; Vico on figurative legal fictions

*Mesotēs* problem: geometrical/mechanical definitions reflect 'philosophical desire to empty life experience' but in SS 1924 'rhetorical kairos as meson in practice counters meson as theory, timeless and naive'
'The study of language as it lives in *Alltäglichkeit* (62) is a consideration of the experience of time, a thick texture of articulated habits, dispositions, and opinions'
Heidegger's rhetorical pessimism — strong critique of optimist theory — 'attracts him, and changes his mind'

subsections.heading: 5. Conclusion: The Uses of the Quarrel of Rhetoric and Philosophy
argumentative_moves: Three things *Rhetoric* does for Heidegger: (1) 'recaptures the original Greek argument in all its incarnate, patho-logical complexity'; (2) 'expresses the Hellenic *endoxa*, and thus serves as an intellectual history'; (3) 'furnishes a way into, an analysis for, the account of life as authentic, the political life'

What philosophers see as weakness must be redescribed as strength: 'rhetoric's analytic strength lies in its limitation to discursive action and capacity'; 'rhetorical focus on *Aussagen*, speaking-out, and on listening as timebound social practice pointed to a range and quality of discursive experience that philosophy had not simply regarded as of little interest, but actively distrusted'
Antifoundationalist defense: rhetoric 'rejects the odd premise that there are "unarticulated thoughts" of a "cabinet of consciousness" — that apolitical piece of furniture'

Pivotal interpretive move on Blattner: 'if Blattner is correct that *Alltäglichkeit* is later eroded by the philosophical program of *Being and Time*, and slides into everydayness, ordinariness, and inauthenticity, in the 1924 lectures the extraordinary emphasis on Hellenic political rhetoric as originary matrix is at the same time an emphasis on *Alltäglichkeit* as timeful, or the solvent of eternity, the mode of eroding the timeless. Timeful politics, whose concepts are in nature, substantiate Heidegger's use of the *Physics* to express an ontology of oscillation between and transformation of potency and act, *dunamis* and *energeia*' — central to BT. 'Blattner asserts that, even later, Heidegger had absolutely no interest in eternity (n. 46)'

'In SS 1924 Heidegger is using the *Rhetoric* not simply to gloss the Aristotelian *Grundbegriffe*, but to force a radical revision of our notion of Aristotle's place in Hellenic inquiry... to use Aristotle's rhetorical revisions as a model or prototype for his own revisions. It is a little alarming to see how intricated the Aristotelian and Heideggerian programs are in SS 1924 — it is very difficult to separate his admiring account from his own revisionary ambitions'

On Heidegger's politics: 'the later relation between Heidegger's philosophy and his politics is a troubling one. My claim is simply that rhetorical hermeneutics enabled him to give lucid, deft accounts of basic political elements in SS 1924' (politically calibrated demurral)

Closing on Kisiel: SS 1924 is 'embarrassment of riches' — felicitous moment whose felicity 'perhaps explain[s] its effacement in later political philosophical moments... arguably, the best twentieth-century reading of Aristotle's *Rhetoric*'. Closing question: 'Is it the case that our political philosophy is difficult because it is insufficiently rhetorical?'

essay_thesis_one_sentence: Heidegger's SS 1924 reading of Aristotle's *Rhetoric* is the volume's most rigorous biological-temporal bridge between Aristotle and *Being and Time*: rhetoric is *not* a *technē* but a *dynamis* (potential) for theorizing the *Alltäglichkeit* of *Miteinandersein* — and *Alltäglichkeit*, properly read, is not 'ordinariness' but 'timefulness,' the political-rhetorical solvent of eternity that colonizes BT's temporal program from within.

key_concepts.name: Alltäglichkeit as timefulness
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Not 'ordinary' but 'timeful' — the timely character of practical life designating the continuous, intermittent, repetitious demands of daily life, its iterability. The vital time-dimension of Dasein and the primary qualification of Miteinandersein. The catalytic agent of temporality in SS 1924 (corrodes foundationalism). Distinct from BT's later slide toward 'everydayness, ordinariness, and inauthenticity' (per Blattner).
key_concepts.pages: 105, 106 (vital time dimension), 110–113 (formulation), 113–115 (qualification of Miteinandersein), 117 (BT colonization), 121 (BT erosion), 125–126 (timeful politics)

key_concepts.name: Rhetoric as dynamis tou theoresai (potentiality for theorizing)
key_concepts.english_form: potentiality for theorizing — NOT a technē
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Rhetoric is 'the inauthentic definition (114)' if defined as technē. Rather, rhetoric is a potentiality, with 'its peculiar time-fraughtness, not an energeia, an actuality.' It is not a complete Wissen; it does not give all information in spite of all teaching manuals. It describes 'the radical incompleteness, the unending, time-ridden task of politics.' Aristotle, Rhetoric 1355b26, glossed at GA 18 122.
key_concepts.function: positive_proposal (defines what rhetoric IS for Heidegger)
key_concepts.pages: 108 (negative def: not technē), 116, 122 (cf. Gadamer Ch 2 p.49)

key_concepts.name: Miteinandersein / Miteinandersprechen
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The primitive, ineluctable, living-with-one-another. Rhetoric handles, discloses 'Miteinandersprechen im Sinne des alltäglichen Miteinanderredens' (GA 18 155). Alltäglichkeit is its primary qualification (BT 178). Not a derived sociality but the ontological structure rhetoric explicitly thematizes.
key_concepts.function: bridge (links Aristotelian discursive politics to BT §29)

key_concepts.name: Kinesis (vital motion of life)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: 'If life, then motion, *kinēsis*. If motion, then time' — Heidegger's signature SS 1924 syllogism. Kinesis 'gives the authentic Da-Charakter to Dasein, the vital place-time of Being.' Ontological significance of passions = our capacity for change, *Veränderlichkeit* of Being. Anchored on Physics 200b12 / GA 18 284 (*archē kinēseōs kai metabolēs*) and 201b27–202a9 (Physics III).
key_concepts.pages: 106 (Physics intrications), 108 (kinesis = 286), 109 (kinesis & Da-Charakter at 287), 112 (Physics 201b27–202a9), 119 (motion as temporal manifold)

key_concepts.name: Pathē as Befindlichkeiten / dispositions oriented to others
key_concepts.german_form: Befindlichkeiten, veränderliche Beschaffenheit, Sichverhalten zu anderen Menschen
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Passions are *not* Wissen, static knowledge, but *Befindlichkeiten* (dispositions, GA 18 232). 'Das *eidos* der *pathē* ist ein Sichverhalten zu anderen Menschen, ein In-der-Welt-Sein' (GA 18 207). They are dispositions oriented on others' dispositions that define our in-the-worldness — *intrinsically social, interpersonal, rather than simply physiological*. Heidegger attributes them to the whole person, not just the soul (122, 192, 197).
key_concepts.pages: 108–110 (Section I.2 on motion-as-pathos), 113 (Hobbes parallel), 113–114 (passion as performative)

key_concepts.name: Phobos as deliberation-inducing pathos
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Phobos has 'peculiar tense, voice, and mode' — future tense, voice subjunctive, mode the possible. *Phobos* as 'already there' (276) as Boden, ground. *kaitoi oudeis bouleuetai peri tōn anelpistōn* (1383a6–8, GA 18 259–260) = 'one does not deliberate about hopeless things'. *Phobos bouleutikous poiei* — fear makes us deliberators. 'Fear as belief (*pistis*)... is essential to rhetorical analysis and crucial to settling affairs.' The *phoberoi* (fearsome ones) define the bearing of Miteinandersein and the polis (GA 18 256–263); contrast with the gentle (*praoi*) and ironic (*eirōnes*).

key_concepts.name: Hexis as ein Wie des pathos
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Hexis is the *Grundbestimmung* of *aretē* (excellence, GA 18 185), basic to Aristotelian ethics. Crucially: hexis is *dynamis*, *Gefasstsein* (185), 'a potential for having; not pure duration but timebound, acquired and lost.' Habit is also 'the *energeia, das eigentliche Da, das Gegenwärtigsein des Habenden und des Gehabten*' (GA 18 174–175); the having of *hekaston*, specific *pathē* as dispositions (192). Hexis is *ein Wie des pathos* (184). 'The movement, or lack of movement, from potency to act describes a basic dimension of moral agency.'
key_concepts.function: bridge (NE II hexis ↔ kinetic potency/act in BT)
key_concepts.pages: 111 (extended treatment), 112 (life modes of active and passive)

key_concepts.name: Kairos / meson / Jeweiligkeit (temporal particularity of practical life)
key_concepts.english_form: timely moment / mean / particular while / respective Dasein
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Kairos is the 'rarely translated into Greek' yet 'indispensable' term of Heidegger's account of Aristotelian *Grundbegriffe* (140); it qualifies *phronēsis* (183) and *praxis* (180). Heidegger shifts *meson* from medicine (geometric/arithmetic, exact) to ethics: *meson für die praxis ist der kairos* (GA 18 144); *meson pros hēmas* (mean-relative-to-us) integrated with kairos. 'Rather meson is *Jeweiligkeit* (temporal particularity — "particular while") in respect to the agent, for Dasein is ever *jeweiliges* (respective) Dasein' (GA 18 201). Pollakis (frequency, GA 18 194) qualifies *ēthikē* over duration.
key_concepts.pages: 110–111, 112 (Mitte object/agent), 119 (kairos again, with Blattner), 123 (meson defined as Jeweiligkeit), 125 (Jeweiligkeit/kairos)

key_concepts.name: Doxa / endoxa / topoi as revisable rhetorical premises
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's lectures on doxa (GA 18 136–158) are 'crucial for the account of politics to be derived from discourse.' The rhetor's purpose is to push Dasein into doxa = continuous pragmatic engagement with time, *Alltäglichkeit* (136). Heidegger reads De anima 428a 20–21 for the *doxa-as-pistis* relation. *Pisteuein* is 'doxa coming to accept'; pistis is not pure belief but that which speaks *for* a thing (138). Doxa/endoxa are the *topoi* both as maxims and as principles of argument (in turn acting as *protaseis* in the enthymeme). 'Heidegger claims doxa is the way we have life in time, not a Wissen, science: Die doxa ist die Weise, in der wir das Leben in seiner Alltäglichkeit da haben (138).' Topoi & endoxa are revisable (have *Revisionsfähigkeit*) in contrast to non-revisable epistēmē.

key_concepts.name: Hearing > speaking (politics of hearing)
key_concepts.german_form: Hören, sich-befindet, Sprechen telos beim Hörer
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: 'Das Sprechen sein telos hat beim "Hörer," beim akroatēs' (GA 18 123); 'Das akouein, "Hören," ist die eigentliche aisthesis' (GA 18 104). The hearer defines the speaker's task — hearer relations writ large are politics. Heidegger's close attention to phenomenology of hearing 'explores temporality as qualifying response, and focuses on living-with-one-another as it transpires.' Aristotle insists on primacy of hearer in determining rhetorical telos (Rhet. 1358b1). Cassin/Narcy on Met. 1006a24–26: responsibility for argument's success rests with listener (*hypomenon*), not with the speaker/demonstrator (*apodeiknys*).
key_concepts.function: positive_proposal (rhetoric as hearing-first, against monologic speaker model)

key_concepts.name: Rhetoric inside politics (innerhalb der politikē)
key_concepts.english_form: rhetoric is inside politics, not adjacent to it
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's GA 18 134: 'Die Rhetorik ist keine auf sich selbst gestellte technē, sondern steht innerhalb der politikē.' Rhetoric is intrinsic, not dependent. Distinct from the parallel claim (GA 18 127): 'Die Ethik gehört in die Politik' (ethics belongs to politics). Rhetoric not as 'handmaiden of politics' but as ontological position internal to politikē. Rhetoric provides the 'hard investigative edge of political inquiry in its capacity to theorize'; its 'basic operations of politics described in Rhetoric 2: creation, alteration, reception of doxa, endoxa, pathē, prohairesis, pisteis, krisis exhaust the limited repertoire of political acts.'

key_concepts.name: Antifoundationalism / radical impurity of mind (Mind is not at all pure)
key_concepts.german_form: Das noein des Menschen ist kein reines
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's antifoundationalism = continuous motion implies continuous impurity. Aristotle attributes passions to whole person, not just soul (GA 18 122, 192, 197); 'Das noein des Menschen ist kein reines' (GA 18 202). Noein dependent on imagination, imagination dependent on bodily sensation; imagination is the *Boden* of *noein* (199). Thus impurity supports *Alltäglichkeit*, timefulness, as hermeneutical focus; impurity prejudices pure duration. Rejection of 'cabinet of consciousness, an enclosed, autonomous intellectual functioning.'
key_concepts.pages: 112 (hexis section close), 113 (de anima 403a3-10), 126 (cabinet of consciousness rejection)

key_concepts.name: Rhetoric colonizes Being and Time
key_concepts.english_form: rhetoric colonizes the philosophical program of Being and Time from within
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Volume-key claim: 'While Heidegger may have thought he had effaced rhetoric in his new philosophical program of *Being and Time*, rhetoric effectively colonized his philosophy from within' (p. 117). Continuity thesis (against Pöggeler's restriction thesis). Per Blattner: BT's manifold-temporality has its origin in SS 1924 reading of Aristotle's Rhetoric.

key_concepts.name: Manifold temporality (non-sequential)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Per Blattner: Dasein's temporality is 'non-sequential manifold of future, present, and past, a complex simultaneity.' BT Division I innovations represent fundamental commitment to a temporal manifold rather than to a linear sequence of past, present, and future 'nows.' Heidegger in SS 1924 'found a very different account of temporality within the political parameters of the Rhetoric' enabling sense of time as simultaneous, intricated, experientially complex.

key_concepts.name: Pollakis (frequency as time-character of ethics)
key_concepts.german_form: Öfter ist gerade dasjenige, was die Zeitlichkeit des Daseins charakterisiert
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger: 'Die Zeitcharakter der ēthikē liegt in pollakis' (GA 18 194) — frequency, not duration. Heidegger 'not only reorients the ethical project away from a consideration of timeless foundational values, but radically affirms the operational value of rhetoric's canon of kairos.' 'Öfter ist gerade dasjenige, was die Zeitlichkeit des Daseins charakterisiert' (191).

key_concepts.name: Antistrophē / paraphyes (rhetoric as offshoot of dialectic)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: 'Rhetoric as offshoot, *paraphyes*, of both dialectic and ethics, displays the practical "cares," pragmatism, that makes it the *antistrophē* of dialectic.' Rhetoric corrects philosophical inquiry by raising temporal development. Cites Aristotle Rhet. opening (1354a1: rhetoric is *antistrophos* tēs dialektikēs).

key_concepts.name: Politics first / political manifold
key_concepts.english_form: political manifold (no pure present, no unmotivated future, no isolated past)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: 'Politics requires simultaneous consideration of past, present, and future dimensions of political action and choice. In politics there is no pure present, no unmotivated future, no isolated past. It is a political manifold — public and accessible.' (p. 121)

key_concepts.name: Authenticity via rhetoric
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: 'Rhetoric gives us the means for and the analysis of authenticity. And there is no part of the political that does not manifest the constraints of time' (p. 124). 'Im eigentlichen kairos' (GA 18 59) as investigative object. Authentic life = political life via rhetorical-temporal analysis.

positions.claim: Aristotle's *Rhetoric*, as Heidegger reads it in SS 1924, *is a life science* (an account of our defining life capacities) — not a manual of speech-manipulation but the *Fundamentallehre vom Logos*, internal to political life.
premises: Human life is defined by possession of language (*logon echon*) — a life fulfilled by use of language, *zoē praktikē meta logon* (GA 18 105)
'Die Rhetorik ist keine auf sich selbst gestellte technē, sondern steht innerhalb der politikē' (GA 18 134)
Rhetoric construes political life, constitutes community (*koinōnia*), claims to *be* politics (GA 18 49, 136)
Heidegger intricates the biological texts (*Parts of Animals*, *Motion of Animals*, GA 18 207–219) with the *Rhetoric* in his discussion of passions as life capacity
targets: Standard reading of Aristotle's *Rhetoric* as *technē* of manipulation
Modern philosophical disregard of Greek biology

positions.claim: *Alltäglichkeit*, properly understood, means *timefulness* — not 'ordinariness' but the timely character of practical life, the catalytic agent of temporality, the primary qualification of *Miteinandersein*.
premises: Heidegger's antifoundationalism: continuous motion implies continuous impurity
Mind is 'not at all pure' (GA 18 202); imagination is the *Boden* of *noein* (199)
'In the SS 1924 program, temporality corrodes foundationalism, and *Alltäglichkeit* is the catalytic agent of temporality'
The BT formula 'Rhetorik [ist]... die erste systematische Hermeneutik der Alltäglichkeit des Miteinanderseins' (BT 178)
targets: Blattner's reading of *Alltäglichkeit* as eroded into 'everydayness, ordinariness, inauthenticity' in BT (corrects Blattner partially)
Generic translation 'everydayness' as 'ordinary'
positions.pages: p. 110–115 (Section I.3–4); p. 121 (Blattner contrast); p. 125 (timeful politics)

positions.claim: Rhetoric is *not a technē* but a *dynamis tou theoresai* — a potentiality-for-theorizing, peculiarly time-fraught, an irrevocably timebound *legein* defined as *pithanon* — and this temporal incompleteness is what makes it the proper instrument for politics.
premises: *Rhetoric* 1355b26 / GA 18 122: rhetoric is *dynamis tou theoresai*
Rhetoric is 'not an *energeia*, an actuality. It is not a complete *Wissen*' (GA 18 113–114)
Aristotelian stipulation of *legein* as *pithanon* (GA 18 116) marks rhetoric as 'irrevocably timebound'
Rhetoric describes 'the radical incompleteness, the unending, time-ridden task of politics'
targets: Manuals/teaching tradition (Hellenistic and medieval rhetoric reduced to school discipline)
Definition of rhetoric as *technē* (the 'inauthentic definition' GA 18 114)
positions.pages: p. 108 (closing of I.1); p. 116 (Section II.1); p. 122 (closing II.2)

positions.claim: If life is motion, and motion is time, then *passions are not Wissen* but *Befindlichkeiten* — dispositions oriented to others' dispositions that define our in-the-worldness; rhetoric is the proper hermeneutic of this affective sociality, and BT's account of *Befindlichkeit* in §29 has its genetic origin in this SS 1924 Aristotelian reading.
premises: 'If life, then motion, *kinēsis*. If motion, then time' (GA 18 286)
Passions are not *Wissen* but *Befindlichkeiten* (GA 18 232)
'Das *eidos* der *pathē* ist ein Sichverhalten zu anderen Menschen, ein In-der-Welt-Sein' (GA 18 207)
Heidegger attributes passions to the *whole person*, not just the soul (GA 18 122, 192, 197)
Hobbes parallel (GA 18 207): emotions defined as intrinsically social, interpersonal, rather than simply physiological
targets: Cartesian-Kantian 'cabinet of consciousness'
Aristotelian *eidos* of *Seele* read as *ousia*

positions.claim: *Kairos* (the timely moment) is the rarely-translated but indispensable term in Heidegger's account of the Aristotelian *Grundbegriffe*; *meson* (the mean) is properly read as *Jeweiligkeit* (temporal particularity), not as geometric mean — and this re-reading makes the *Rhetoric* canon of kairos the operational center of practical-philosophical analysis.
premises: *Kairos*: 'The character of *Besorgen*, the indispensable... term of Heidegger's account of the Aristotelian *Grundbegriffe*' (GA 18 140)
Kairos qualifies *phronēsis* (GA 18 183) and *praxis*: 'Die Handlung selbst hat ihr telos im kairos' (GA 18 189)
*Meson für die praxis ist der kairos* (GA 18 144) = sharp commentary on virtue of prudence
'Die Zeitcharakter der ēthikē liegt in pollakis' (GA 18 194) — frequency, not duration
targets: Geometrical/arithmetic *mesotēs* as timeless mean (foundation as boast)
Foundationalist accounts of Greek ethics ('late, extraneous applications of the *Grundbegriffe*')
positions.pages: p. 110–112 (extended treatment); p. 119 (Section II.3); p. 123–125 (Politics First)

positions.claim: Heidegger's antifoundationalism — 'mind is not at all pure' (GA 18 202), the impurity of *noein* through imagination/sensation — is rhetorical-genealogical: rhetoric requires Aristotle's life-science attribution of passions to the whole person, and BT's later 'cabinet of consciousness' rejection has its rhetorical origin here.
premises: 'Das *noein des Menschen ist kein reines* (GA 18 202)'
Imagination depends on bodily sensation; imagination is the *Boden* of *noein* (GA 18 199)
'Die Rhetorik bekommt also die Sphäre, in der das Leben sich bewegt' [implied]
'Continuous motion implies continuous impurity'
targets: Cartesian/Kantian model of mind
Aristotelian *eidos der Seele* as *ousia* taken for entification (GA 18 30)

positions.claim: Hearing has priority over speaking — the 'politics of hearing' rhetorically grounds the BT analysis of *Hören* as *eigentliche aisthesis* (GA 18 104) and BT §34 (Mitteilen/Reden), against any monologic-speaker model.
premises: 'Das Sprechen sein telos hat beim "Hörer," beim akroatēs' (GA 18 123)
'Das akouein, "Hören," ist die eigentliche aisthesis' (GA 18 104)
Rhetoric 1358b1: primacy of hearer in determining rhetorical *telos*
Cassin/Narcy on Met. 1006a24–26: responsibility for argument's success rests with listener (*hypomenon*)
Heidegger's frequent use of *Rhetoric* offers analysis of different possibilities of *sich-befinden* of the hearer (GA 18 169)
targets: Monologic, timeless philosophical address (the 'inadequate philosophical model')
Speech-act theory absent rhetorical-temporal phenomenology

positions.claim: Rhetoric *colonizes* Being and Time from within: Heidegger thought he had effaced rhetoric in his new philosophical program, but BT's manifold-temporality, *Befindlichkeit*, *Sorge*, and *Sein-zum-Tode* all have their genetic origin in SS 1924's rhetorical reading of Aristotle.
premises: 'I have argued that a careful reading of the *Rhetoric* allowed Heidegger to exploit its initiatives as a powerful revisionary force in his account of Greek inquiry'

'In *Being and Time* that Heidegger claims that *Alltäglichkeit* as timeful character of Dasein in its living-with-another defines rhetorical hermeneutic. Therefore Heidegger's fascination with the *Rhetoric* becomes, first in SS 1924, and then in *Being and Time*, a series of elaborations of the timeful as modifying care, and reception'
Per Blattner: BT's manifold-temporality is the 'fundamental commitment' that Heidegger's SS 1924 sourced from rhetorical reading of *Rhetoric*
SS 1925 GA 20 contains 'diffuse echoes of the rhetorical formulae of SS 1924'
targets: Pöggeler's restriction thesis (Ch 7)
Reading of *Alltäglichkeit* as 'eroded' in BT (corrects Blattner partially while accepting his temporal manifold)
positions.pages: p. 117 (Section II.2 opening); p. 121 (Section II.3.A close); p. 122 (Section II.3.C); p. 126 (Conclusion)

positions.claim: A 'Heideggerian politics of time' appears in SS 1924, perhaps hypothesized by Arendt's early fascination with Heidegger — politics as no pure present, no unmotivated future, no isolated past, but a 'political manifold.'
premises: Heidegger reads two Aristotelian statements: ethics belongs to politics (GA 18 127); rhetoric is inside politics (GA 18 134)
'Rhetoric provides the hard investigative edge of political inquiry in its capacity to theorize, and give an account of the basic transactions of politics; it is intrinsic, not dependent'
Rhetoric 2 operations (*doxa, endoxa, pathē, prohairesis, pisteis, krisis*) 'exhaust the limited repertoire of political acts'
Political time is minute (Dasein experiences only appropriate or inappropriate nows)
targets: Stanley Fish's 'inspired adhoccery' (insufficient temporality)
Arendt's later anti-rhetorical framing (only her *early* fascination acknowledged)
Foundationalist political philosophy

positions.claim: What philosophers see as rhetoric's weakness must be redescribed as its strength: rhetoric's analytic limitation to *discursive action and capacity* is precisely its disclosive power — rhetoric rejects the 'odd premise that there are unarticulated thoughts of a cabinet of consciousness.'
premises: 'Rhetorical focus on *Aussagen*, speaking-out, and on listening as timebound social practice pointed to a range and quality of discursive experience that philosophy had not simply regarded as of little interest, but actively distrusted'
Rhetoric 'rejects the odd premise that there are unarticulated thoughts of a cabinet of consciousness — that apolitical piece of furniture'
Rhetoric's strength is its 'self-limitation to acts of articulation'

If Blattner correct that Alltäglichkeit eroded later, in 1924 'extraordinary emphasis on Hellenic political rhetoric as originary matrix is at the same time an emphasis on Alltäglichkeit as timeful, or the solvent of eternity, the mode of eroding the timeless'
targets: Philosophical reception of rhetoric as 'amoral fixation on discursive persuasion with no sense of timeless truths'
Cabinet-of-consciousness model of mind (Cartesian)
Theoretical fascination with textuality, undecidability, immortality

positions.claim: It is alarming how intricated the Aristotelian and Heideggerian programs are in SS 1924 — Heidegger is using Aristotle's rhetorical revisions as model for his own revisions; rhetorical hermeneutics enabled him to give 'lucid, deft accounts of basic political elements,' though the later relation between Heidegger's philosophy and his politics is 'troubling.'
premises: 'In SS 1924 Heidegger is using the *Rhetoric* not simply to gloss the Aristotelian *Grundbegriffe*, but to force a radical revision of our notion of Aristotle's place in Hellenic inquiry'
Heidegger uses Aristotle's rhetorical revisions 'as a model or prototype for his own revisions'
'It is very difficult to separate his admiring account from his own revisionary ambitions'
targets: Reading SS 1924 as straightforward exegesis (it is also self-revision)
Avoidance of Heidegger's politics in interpreting his rhetoric (acknowledged but minimized)

positions.claim: SS 1924 is, per Kisiel, an 'embarrassment of riches' — felicitous moment whose felicity may explain its effacement in later political-philosophical moments — but is 'arguably, the best twentieth-century reading of Aristotle's *Rhetoric*.' The closing question: is our political philosophy difficult because it is insufficiently rhetorical?
premises: Kisiel's Genesis claim of SS 1924's pivotal status
Twentieth-century philosophical political language inadequate to account for time
The 'meditations on time' of SS 1924 are politically and historically minute in a way later Heidegger and later 20th-century philosophy is not
targets: 20th-century political philosophy more broadly (Habermas, Rawls implicitly)
Heidegger's own later abandonment (echoes VT1 with Pöggeler, but argues it as effacement of riches)

interlocutors.role: Struever's main interlocutor for time. *Heidegger's Temporal Idealism* (Cambridge UP 1999) supplies the framework of Dasein's temporality as 'non-sequential manifold' — Struever appropriates this manifold reading and *traces it back to SS 1924's rhetorical Aristotle*, partially correcting Blattner's claim that Alltäglichkeit erodes into ordinariness in BT.

interlocutors.name: Pierre Aubenque
interlocutors.role: French Aristotelian. Per his 'Logos et pathos: Pour une définition dialectique des passions' (in *Corps et âme: sur le De anima*, ed. Viano, Vrin 1996, 37–49), claims *Rhetoric* delivers a 'fully rhetorized psychology' with topics already organized for argument. Per *Le problème de l'être chez Aristote* (PUF 1994), calls rhetoric a 'practical anthropology.' Aubenque also tracks 'pre-Platonic program' that Aristotle takes over from the Sophists.
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed (rhetorized-psychology gloss); refined (Heidegger 'pushes Sophistic notions further' — orientation to *unbedingt*)

interlocutors.name: P. Christopher Smith
interlocutors.role: *Hermeneutics of Original Argument: Demonstration, Dialectic, Rhetoric* (Northwestern 1998). Provides the 'embodied argument as patho/logical' framing — incarnation as motif in Aristotle. Smith's 'original argument' thesis: Hellenic culture as matrix; logical and chronological priority of dialectic and rhetoric over scientific demonstration.

interlocutors.name: Michel Meyer
interlocutors.role: French rhetorician. Per *Histoire de la rhétorique des grecs à nos jours* (Lib. Gén. Fr. 1999) and his 'Postface' to *Aristote: Rhétorique; des passions* (Rivages 1989). Meyer thematizes history of rhetoric as 'succession of shifts in dominance in the relations of the three complementary concerns of ethos, pathos, and logos.' Meyer's 'problematological' nature of rhetoric: rhetoric flourishes in lack of system. Politics as 'constant motion, as the process of negotiating differences and distances through discursive interventions.'
interlocutors.citations: Notes 5 (Lib. Gén. Fr. 1999), 6 (Rivages 1989), 16 (136), 7 (in 'pathos eine Bestimmung des Seienden mit dem Charakter der Veränderlichkeit')

interlocutors.name: Klaus Dockhorn
interlocutors.role: German rhetorician. Reviewed Gadamer's *Wahrheit und Methode* (1st ed.) in *Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen* 218 (1966): 169–206. Per Dockhorn, Aristotle's three kinds of proof (*ethos, pathos, logos*) — pertaining to speaker, audience, text — exhaust the category of 'commonsense', the intersubjectively shared communal beliefs in *koinoi topoi*. Heidegger sees rhetoric not as teaching-manual tradition but as 'second formation, indeed alternate formation to philosophy.'

interlocutors.name: Wilhelm Dilthey
interlocutors.role: Heidegger's immediate philosophical background; the only modern thinker (per Heidegger via Struever) who recognized 'this vital historical initiative' (i.e., the rhetorical *Affektenlehre* tradition). Dilthey's *Weltanschauung und Analyse des Menschen seit Renaissance und Reformation* (vol. 2 of *Gesammelte Schriften*, 1960). Per Makkreel, Dilthey's temporality is realist; Dilthey's time derived from *Innewerden* (inner becoming), not Kantian *Vorstellen* (representative consciousness).

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: Internal — Struever's 'timefulness' reading of *Alltäglichkeit* against Blattner's 'erosion-into-ordinariness' thesis
tensions_and_open_questions.description: Struever cites Blattner approvingly for the manifold-temporality reading of BT, but explicitly resists Blattner's claim that 'Alltäglichkeit is later eroded by the philosophical program of Being and Time' into 'everydayness, ordinariness, inauthenticity.' She concedes the *possibility* of such erosion but argues that in 1924 'extraordinary emphasis on Hellenic political rhetoric as originary matrix is at the same time an emphasis on Alltäglichkeit as timeful, or the solvent of eternity.' The titular 'timefulness' is Struever's coined corrective.
tensions_and_open_questions.interp_marker: [INTERP-low] — Struever explicitly resists Blattner; characterizing this as a 'tension' (rather than a flat refutation) reflects the analyst's reading of the essay's hedging

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: Cross-essay — Struever supports Gross's continuity thesis (HR-01-GROSS-A/B) against Pöggeler's restriction thesis (HR-07-POGGELER)
tensions_and_open_questions.description: Both Struever and Gross share the GA 18 110 epigraph and BT 178 epigraph; both argue rhetoric is central to BT (genetic link). Struever's Position P8 ('Rhetoric colonizes Being and Time') directly conflicts with Pöggeler's titular thesis. The volume's frame (Gross opening + Pöggeler closing) sets up a productive disagreement; Struever's essay sits squarely on the Gross side.

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: Cross-essay — Struever's politically-rich reading is *compatible* with Kisiel's protopolitics (HR-06-KISIEL)
tensions_and_open_questions.description: Both Struever and Kisiel read SS 1924 as politically-loaded. Struever: 'a Heideggerian politics of time appears, even if briefly, in SS 1924 — a politics perhaps hypothesized by Arendt in her early fascination with Heidegger' (p. 124). Kisiel reads SS 1924 as 'rhetorical protopolitics' with Arendtian afterlife. The two essays converge on the political register of GA 18 §§25–28 / kinesis / Aussagen reading.

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: Cross-essay — Heidegger's politics: troubling acknowledgment without full engagement
tensions_and_open_questions.description: Struever explicitly notes 'the later relation between Heidegger's philosophy and his politics is a troubling one' (p. 126), but her claim is 'simply that rhetorical hermeneutics enabled him to give lucid, deft accounts of basic political elements in SS 1924.' This is more politically-engaged than HR-02-GADAMER (who concedes Heidegger 'erred' politically without connecting to rhetoric) but less politically-engaged than HR-06-KISIEL (who tracks the metontological/archaic-poietic phases) or HR-01-GROSS-B (Section IV addresses 1933 explicitly).
tensions_and_open_questions.interp_marker: [INTERP-low] — Struever's hedge is explicit but comparatively understated; the 'tension' is between her positive rhetorical-political claim and her demurral on Heidegger's later politics

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: Within-Heidegger — does *Alltäglichkeit* in BT mean 'timefulness' or 'ordinariness'?
tensions_and_open_questions.description: GA 18 110 / BT 178: rhetoric is the 'first systematic hermeneutic of the Alltäglichkeit of Miteinandersein.' But BT also treats Alltäglichkeit through the *fallenness* register (Verfallen, das Man, Gerede). Struever argues these registers are reconcilable IF *Alltäglichkeit* means *timefulness*: the 'solvent of eternity' that is itself the catalyst of authentic temporality, not its opposite.

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: Internal — *eidos der pathē* (GA 18 207) vs. mind 'not at all pure' (GA 18 202): Aristotle entified vs. de-entified

edges.target: CONCEPT:Rhetoric as dynamis tou theoresai (potentiality for theorizing)
edges.note: Rhetoric can colonize BT only because it is a *potentiality* (not a complete Wissen) — its time-fraughtness is what equips it to be the genetic source of BT's existential-temporal program.

Struever's continuity thesis (rhetoric colonizes BT from within) directly supports Gross's titular framing ('Heidegger relocates rhetoric at the heart of his fundamental ontology'). Both essays share the GA 18 110 epigraph + BT 178 epigraph. Volume-level alignment with HR-01 (intro frame).
Struever's continuity thesis directly opposes Pöggeler's 'restricted conception' thesis — the volume's titular disagreement (VT1). Both cite GA 18 but read its trajectory diametrically.

Struever's politics-of-time reading ('a Heideggerian politics of time appears in SS 1924 — perhaps hypothesized by Arendt') aligns with Kisiel's 'rhetorical protopolitics' reading. Both treat SS 1924 as politically pivotal; both name Arendt as Heidegger's political-philosophical heir.

Both Struever and Gadamer agree rhetoric is *dynamis*, not *technē*. Struever specifies the Aristotelian phrase: *dynamis tou theoresai* (Rhet. 1355b26 / GA 18 122) — narrowing Gadamer's broader *dynamis*-claim into a specific textual anchor.

Struever's reading of pathē as 'Befindlichkeiten oriented to others' (GA 18 207, 232) supports Gross's pathos-as-substrate genealogy in HR-01-GROSS-B (Section IV). Both reject the cabinet-of-consciousness model. The two essays share the hermeneutic framing of Aristotelian pathē as ontologically primary.

GA 18 110 (epigraph 1: 'Rhetorik ist nichts anderes als die Auslegung des konkreten Daseins, die Hermeneutik des Dasein selbst') is the SS 1924 source of BT 178 (epigraph 2: 'Rhetorik [ist]... die erste systematische Hermeneutik der Alltäglichkeit des Miteinanderseins'). The continuity is identification, not analogy.

BT 178's claim that rhetoric is 'first systematic hermeneutic of Alltäglichkeit' operationalizes Aristotle's Rhet. 1355b26 (rhetoric as *dynamis tou theoresai*) — through GA 18 122. The Aristotelian-Greek source becomes BT's existential-hermeneutic frame.

GA 18 286 ('If life, then motion, kinēsis... Sein-als-Bewegtsein') operationalizes Physics 200b12 (*archē kinēseōs kai metabolēs*) — Aristotelian *physis* as motion-principle becomes Heidegger's life-time foundation. Cf. GA 18 284 (Physics 200b12 explicitly cited).

GA 18 207–219 (lectures of July 3 and 4) intricates Aristotle's biological texts (*De motu animalium*, *De partibus animalium*) with the *Rhetoric* in discussing passions as life-capacity. Heidegger's account of pathē presupposes Aristotle's biological zoology — UNIQUE to this volume.

GA 18 207–219 with *De partibus animalium*. Heidegger's pathē-as-Sichverhalten presupposes Aristotle's biological treatment of life-capacities. Unique cross-pipeline candidate (Aristotle pipeline lacks PA-01).

GA 18 232 ('passions are not Wissen but Befindlichkeiten, dispositions') is the genetic source of BT §29 (*Befindlichkeit*). The Aristotelian-rhetorical reading of pathē directly seeds BT's existential ontology.
GA 18 123 ('Sprechen sein telos hat beim Hörer') operationalizes Rhet. 1358b1 (primacy of hearer in determining rhetorical telos). Hearing-priority claim grounds politics-of-hearing reading.

GA 18 246–263 (lectures of July 14–15) operationalizes Aristotle's Rhet. 1382a20–22 (fear as 'pain or disturbance from mental picture of future evil') and 1382b21–22 (*phobos bouleutikous poiei*) and 1383a6–8 (*kaitoi oudeis bouleuetai peri tōn anelpistōn*). Phobos's tense (future) and mode (subjunctive/possible) is the most-developed pathos-temporal reading of SS 1924.

GA 18 144 ('meson für die praxis ist der kairos') refines Aristotle's NE 1106a26f (the rhetorical account of meson). Heidegger shifts the Aristotelian *meson* from medical/geometric mean to *kairos*-as-Jeweiligkeit — temporal particularity over arithmetic exactness.
GA 18 184–185 (hexis as Grundbestimmung of arete; hexis as 'Wie des pathos') refines NE II's account of hexis. Heidegger reads Aristotelian hexis as dynamis (Gefasstsein), timebound and lossable.

GA 18 134 ('Rhetorik steht innerhalb der politikē') vs. GA 18 127 ('Die Ethik gehört in die Politik'): rhetoric is *intrinsic* to politics; ethics merely *belongs* to politics. The contrast articulates rhetoric's special ontological position. Section II.4 'Politics First.'
GA 20 (SS 1925) defines rhetoric as 'first part of logic, rightly understood' (264) — a 'diffuse echo' of GA 18 110's identification of rhetoric with Dasein-hermeneutic. Continuity into 1925.
Blattner's *Heidegger's Temporal Idealism* is Struever's main interlocutor for the manifold-temporality reading of BT (notes 11, 25–35 = 13 citations).
